---
title: "Adjusting biases in origin-destination flows"
---

All six adjustment methods remain available. Choose a method based on the
available coverage, benchmark and covariate information:

| Method | Main information used |
| --- | --- |
| Inverse penetration | Population and active-user counts |
| Selection rate | Benchmark flows and area covariates |
| Selection rate II | Benchmark origin/destination margins |
| Raking ratio | Benchmark margins and iterative balancing |
| Coefficient | Fitted relationship between observed and benchmark flows |
| Multilevel | Flow, population, distance and bias predictors |

Run all methods on the Census subset using a fixed-effect frequentist model:

```python
from debiaspy import adjust_all_methods, debiaspy_example_data

bundle = debiaspy_example_data(n_areas=25)
adjustments = adjust_all_methods(
    bundle["mpd_od"],
    bundle["coverage"],
    benchmark_od_df=bundle["benchmark_od"],
    covariates_df=bundle["covariates"],
    distance_df=bundle["distance"],
    methods="all",
    multilevel_engine="frequentist",
    multilevel_args={"random_intercept": "none", "prediction_scope": "observed"},
)
print(adjustments["inverse_penetration"].head())
```

Each result retains OD identifiers and has `flow_adj`. Method-specific
arguments can be supplied through the corresponding `*_args` dictionary.
For example, `inverse_penetration_args={"weight_by": "origin"}` selects origin
weights. Use `methods=["inverse_penetration", "raking_ratio"]` to run a subset.

Keep the same counting unit, time period and source scope across observed and
benchmark flows. Zero-user inverse weights can produce infinite flows; inspect
and resolve these rows before interpreting aggregate metrics. Calibration on a
benchmark should be evaluated with independent data when assessing predictive
accuracy. The example's coverage uses its benchmark margins.

The multilevel function accepts `formula=` or the paired `mobility_formula=`
and `bias_formula=` inputs. The deprecated R `custom_formula` spelling is omitted
from this new Python interface. Bayesian engines remain experimental; see
[Bayesian adjustment](t09-advanced-bayesian-adjustment.qmd).
